<reason>Both sides were strong, disciplined, and format-compliant (clean Q1/Q2 and A1:/A2: labels on both sides). CON's rebuttal execution was arguably the sharper of the two: the "opt-in is a price for refusing, not a right to refuse" line, the Q2 dilemma that extracted PRO's admission that the load-bearing bundling ban is a non-waivable collective term, and the casting-specific dismantling of PRO's anti-retaliation remedy (no vacancy record, no duty to explain) all landed real damage. But PRO ends the exchange with the more central surviving route. PRO neutralized both of CON's opening pillars: the "stranger's voice already" counterfactual was answered by the attribution/timbre distinction (audiences believe the actor themselves emoted, so greater similarity is greater exposure), and the hostage story was defeated by separability (a no to cloning still leaves the century-old human dub, so nothing blocks the Polish or Tagalog release). CON rebuilt the hostage point as hybrid-pipeline friction, which is plausible but more speculative than the original claim. Meanwhile the harm at the heart of the motion goes largely unanswered against CON: CON's package (floors, residuals, disclosure, model-retention bans) still permits a synthetic performance nobody consented to, and CON's replies address only the weak performer's inability to use a consent right — never why the performer with leverage should also lose the ability to say no. PRO also absorbed CON's instrument ("the floor sets what a yes must cost; only the person decides if yes happens"), making its world close to inclusive of CON's, so CON needed to prove the added consent right is affirmatively harmful, and the visibility/blacklisting mechanism, while plausible, was asserted more than demonstrated. Thin but real edge to PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Q2 dilemma ("is your opt-in waivable at hire?") plus B4.4-B4.6 was the most surgical sequence, forcing PRO to concede that the protective element is a non-waivable collective term and exposing the weakness of the retaliation remedy in a discretionary casting market. The most decisive rebuttal for the outcome, though, was PRO's A2.2-A2.3 attribution answer to CON's dubbing counterfactual — distinguishing an openly different dub artist from a clone that sells the illusion the actor spoke and intended those sounds — which removed CON's main attack on PRO's harm story and left "paid impersonation is still impersonation" standing through the closing.</best_rebuttal>
